findings.title: Block match stats are rolled back or double-counted
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? increments match_count and calls save while EmailValidator is running inside User validation. UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save, so the counter is updated twice. user.save wraps validations in a transaction, and when the email is rejected that transaction rolls back the BlockedEmail write. With call_discourse_hub off, a real blocked signup therefore leaves match_count and last_match_at unchanged; with it on, only the outer valid? write sticks. The model specs call should_block? directly, so they never see this and the block statistics are wrong in production.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is an exact, case-sensitive match
findings.body: should_block? looks up BlockedEmail.where(email: email) with the raw address and no downcase or strip. Postgres unique/equality on string is case-sensitive, and nothing in User.new_from_params or EmailValidator normalizes the address before this check. A row for bad@spam.com will not match Bad@spam.com or " bad@spam.com ", so a blocked address can still register by changing case or adding whitespace. The unique index has the same problem, so both casings can be stored as separate rows.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is unanchored
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})") after only escaping dots, with no end anchor and no escape of other metacharacters. A whitelist entry gmail.com therefore matches user@gmail.com.evil.test (and any longer suffix), so the signup is treated as allowed. A blacklist entry can also false-positive on addresses that merely contain that domain string after @. This is the only domain check on User now that email_validator was removed, and the new spec stubs should_block? and never covers it.
